A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modular ObjectNav study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gibson experiments and component ablations, a five-person human baseline, and analysis of 1,000 navigation episodes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds HM3D evaluations, frontier-selection, PPO-clipping and height-map experiments, and qualitative navigation cases.

M1.justification: v2 introduces tested procedure variants using detector-plus-SAM2 segmentation, nearest/farthest frontier selection, and a height-map channel replacing the binary obstacle channel. These extend the framework; its principal architecture, reward functions and test-time algorithms remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 extends the Gibson navigation evaluation to HM3D, using five test scenes for perception comparisons and the full 20-scene HM3D v1 validation split for component evaluation (A.4). This materially broadens environmental coverage. MP3D and AI2-THOR evaluations remain proposed future work.

E2.justification: Table 1 substantially expands perception comparisons by adding RF-DETR-Seg, RF-DETR+SAM2 and YOLO11-XL under both corner and frontier policies. The new HM3D comparison also evaluates YOLO11-N. Table 4 retains the same ten named prior navigation baselines and the human baseline.

E3.justification: New experiments specify five-scene detector testing, 20-scene zero-shot testing without retraining, FPS reporting, and PPO clipping settings of 0.2 and 0.001. These extend the established evaluation procedures. The original 500-step limit, dynamic-step calculation, success criterion, navigation metrics and two-million-frame training budget remain unchanged; expanded human-study controls are newly disclosed details.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of frontier-goal selection, PPO update constraints and height information (Tables 7–9), plus cross-dataset component ablations on HM3D (Table 6). New Figures 7–9 illustrate untrapping, dynamic-goal and remapping behavior. The original failure analysis and perception visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates; the expanded human-study description introduces no new statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Retained Gibson results are unchanged, including the continuous policy's 84.4% SR/48.2% SPL and humans' 98.0% SR/53.3% SPL. Substantial new results appear in the expanded Table 1 and Tables 5–9: RF-DETR-Seg obtains 52.4% SR/24.2% SPL on five HM3D scenes, and the height-map ablation reports 75.1% SR versus 78.3% with the obstacle map. These are added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The reward definitions, map and action formulations, and dynamic-step equation remain unchanged. The new PPO and height-map discussions provide empirical analysis and intuitive explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 qualifies v1's claim that policy improvements yield only marginal gains: the abstract now says perception and test-time strategies often yield larger gains, while the introduction and conclusion emphasize reliable policy comparisons under unified configurations. The conclusion drops the 'first' empirical-study claim. The central decomposition, performance and human-gap contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning cross-dataset transfer, frontier information-gain/travel-cost trade-offs, restrictive PPO updates, and why height information may require more training data. It also proposes that structured maps explain similar CNN/Transformer performance. Some interpretations overreach: A.4 asserts a shared detector ordering that is not consistent across the metrics in Tables 1 and 5.

D1.justification: v2 supplies project and repository links, explicitly identifies PPO, and expands human-study documentation with the interface, observation restrictions and prohibition on repeated episodes. These clarify existing work without establishing that the human experiment changed. Hardware and training-budget disclosures are retained; release wording remains inconsistent between the introduction and A.2.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to MOPA for random/frontier goal selection, PPO and broader robotics learning, contemporary detectors, and 3D-LLM/ForesightNav for spatial representations. These broaden supporting context and attribution while retaining the central positioning as an empirical study of modular ObjectNav components.

P1.justification: The abstract, conclusion and most recommendation passages are rewritten, and policy-learning and human-study explanations are expanded. Numbered experimental subsubsections become paragraph headings, the appendix is reorganized, and references move after the appendix. These constitute extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–9 and Figures 7–10, expands Table 1, and redraws Figure 2 with failure-mode annotations. Table 4 becomes a full-width summary containing one own-policy row instead of four; the other policies' results remain elsewhere. Typography, margins, headers and recommendation boxes change throughout, while original perception Figures 7–9 reappear as Figures 11–13.

improvement.justification: v1's broad design recommendations rested on Gibson evaluations. v2 substantially strengthens their empirical basis through HM3D testing, including 20-scene zero-shot component ablations, and targeted tests of additional policy-design assumptions. Clearer human-study documentation also improves assessability. The overgeneralized detector-ranking claim and continued absence of uncertainty estimates limit interpretation, but the new validation materially improves support for the paper's central conclusions.
